analysis.one_liner: Caps the wage the Labor Department can require growers to pay guest farmworkers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House Judiciary subcommittee without a hearing or vote, leaving the federal wage floor for guest farmworkers untouched.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the H-2A guest farmworker program, the Labor Department currently requires growers to pay a federally set wage rate that is meant to be high enough that hiring foreign workers does not drag down pay for U.S. farmworkers. This bill would have set a cap: the Department could never require a grower to pay more than the local prevailing wage for seasonal farmwork or the federal or state minimum wage, whichever is higher. It also let growers use wage surveys they or their industry funded to set that "prevailing wage," and pay by piece rate so long as the workforce average met the wage. The bill never moved past a House subcommittee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural employers who use the H-2A guest worker program would have gained, because the bill capped the wage the Labor Department can force them to pay. The federal guest-worker wage rate they currently must pay — designed to keep cheap foreign labor from undercutting U.S. farmworkers — is generally higher than the local prevailing wage the bill would have allowed, so the cap would have meant lower labor costs, plus the flexibility to pay by piece rate and to rely on industry-funded wage surveys.

how_it_helps.text: It barred the Labor Department from requiring an H-2A employer to pay more than the greater of the local prevailing wage for seasonal farmwork or the federal or state minimum wage — replacing the higher guest-worker wage rate with a lower ceiling.
It let growers obtain a prevailing-wage determination from the state employment agency, or rely on wage surveys conducted or funded by themselves or groups of employers.
It allowed growers to pay by piece rate, task rate, or other incentive methods, as long as the group's average hourly earnings met the prevailing wage.

analysis.who_pays: The workers would have paid. H-2A visa holders and U.S. farmworkers alike would have faced a lower wage floor, since the required wage could fall to the 51st-percentile prevailing wage and be determined partly by surveys funded by the employers themselves. U.S. farmworkers' pay could also have been undercut by an expanded supply of lower-cost guest labor.

drawbacks.text: The bill let an employer satisfy the prevailing-wage requirement using wage surveys 'conducted or funded by the employer or a group of employers,' meaning the growers seeking to pay lower wages could supply the evidence used to set those wages.

It would have allowed piece-rate and other incentive pay as long as the average hourly earnings of the whole workforce met the prevailing wage, so individual workers could legally earn less than the required hourly rate.

By capping the required wage at the 51st-percentile prevailing wage, the bill would have eliminated the higher federal guest-worker wage floor that exists precisely to keep an influx of lower-cost foreign labor from pulling down pay for U.S. farmworkers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit to the public was essentially nothing: it would have lowered a legally required wage floor for some of the country's lowest-paid workers — many of them foreign guest workers with little bargaining power — in order to cut labor costs for agricultural employers. It also built in weak safeguards: growers could get the "prevailing wage" from surveys they or their trade groups funded themselves, and piece-rate pay only had to average out at the required wage across the whole workforce, allowing individual slow pickers to earn less. The only honest argument for it was that growers face genuine labor-cost pressure and that the federal guest-worker wage floor may be higher than local market wages — but the burden of the fix would have fallen on workers who already earn near the bottom of the wage scale. Its death kept the floor intact.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its immigration subcommittee, and never got a hearing or a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 3, 2003 and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
On May 5, 2003 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security, and Claims, where it stayed with no further action.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred; the last entry in the bill's action history is the May 2003 subcommittee referral, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Guest and domestic farmworkers are better off, because the existing federal wage floor for H-2A agricultural workers stayed in place. Agricultural employers gained nothing, but lost nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farmworkers — the wage floor stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Virgil H. Goode Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap the wage growers can be required to pay H-2A guest farmworkers.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill; after the May 2003 referral to the immigration subcommittee, no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: 16 of the bill's 17 cosponsors were Republicans; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers using H-2A guest workers
industries.note: The bill would have cut growers' labor costs by capping the wage the Labor Department can require for H-2A guest workers below the current federal floor, and by letting growers influence the wage determination through their own surveys. It matters for ordinary people because that floor is what keeps a large supply of lower-cost foreign labor from dragging down farm wages generally.

industries.industry: Migrant and seasonal farmworkers (guest and domestic)
industries.note: Both H-2A visa workers and U.S. farmworkers would have faced a lower wage floor — the cap, the employer-funded wage surveys, and the piece-rate averaging could all push hourly earnings below what the current rules guarantee. Farmworkers are among the lowest-paid workers in the country, and the existing wage floor is one of the few protections they have.
